query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Stability and self-repair of a passivating surface layer, enabled by carefully tuned passivating-element (e.g., Cr) content, predominantly governs the resistance of high-entropy alloys to combined wear and corrosion in harsh environments.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline AlCoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy in an as-cast, homogenized condition with a standard (middle-range) Cr content suitable for forming passive films.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary Cr content in a series of AlCoCrFeNi alloys (e.g., from 5 at.% up to 25 at.%) while keeping the other element concentrations constant.
generation.conditions: Perform tribocorrosion tests in a chloride-rich (3.5 wt.% NaCl) environment under moderate normal load (~5 N) and sliding speed (~0.2 m/s), at room temperature, for a fixed duration (~4 hours).
generation.structural_mediator: Formation, disruption, and re-formation (repassivation) rates of the oxide-based protective layer influenced by the Cr content.
generation.mechanism: Higher Cr levels enhance passivation kinetics, forming stable, protective oxide films that mitigate both corrosive attack and mechanical abrasion at the sliding interface, thereby limiting net tribocorrosion damage.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline, alloys optimized for passivation (e.g., with moderate to high Cr) will exhibit a measurable decrease in the combined mass loss or volume loss from simultaneous wear and corrosion. In separate measurements, both the corrosion rate and wear track depth (and friction coefficient) should be reduced for these higher-Cr variants compared to the baseline.
generation.baseline: A composition with mid-range Cr content (e.g., the typical AlCoCrFeNi) under the same tribocorrosion test parameters, used to quantify and compare wear and corrosion separately and in combination.
generation.boundary: If the environment changes to a solvent or pH in which Cr-based passive films are unstable, or if mechanical loading becomes large enough to disrupt passivating layers faster than they can reform, the hypothesis may not hold.
generation.uncertainty: Although literature supports the role of passivation, the exact optimal Cr content and interactions with other elements are not yet fully established; further experiments are needed to confirm and refine the threshold where passivation dominates tribocorrosion behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Manufacture multiple AlCoCrFeNi alloys with varied Cr content (including zero Cr as a negative control) and subject each to in situ tribocorrosion tests in a chloride solution under identical mechanical loads, comparing simultaneous wear-corrosion rates.
measurements: Electrochemical polarization to gauge real-time corrosion current
Wear track profiling to determine volume loss and friction coefficient
Surface and cross-sectional microstructural analysis (SEM/EDX/XRD) to evaluate oxide formation and integrity
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If an alloy with reduced or negligible Cr content exhibits equal or better combined wear-corrosion resistance under the same test conditions as a high-Cr alloy, it would falsify the proposed mechanism that passivation driven by Cr content is primary in controlling tribocorrosion resistance.

cited_evidence.text: It was found that, by reducing the Mn concentration (to 5 at.% Mn), the CoCrFeMnNi alloy acquires higher yield strength values after annealing at 1117 K (from 387 to 477 MPa) due to the grain refinement effect (from 4.4 to 2.61 µm) []. Mn also shows a rapid evaporation effect during melting processes; hence, in our study, this element was replaced by Mo, which could improve the resistance to high temperatures []. Co–Cr–Mo alloy is widely used for manufacturing of vanes and gas turbines due to its excellent fatigue behavior and wear resistance [,,,]. In such alloys, molybdenum has a beneficial effect on passivation capacity, contributing to the formation of a protective surface layer that allows pitting corrosion to be limited [,]. Studies were conducted to estimate the effects on the microstructure and properties of alloys with different Mo contents [,,]. Such alloys have been designed for the manufacture of furnace casings and chemical tanks used in high-temperature and corrosion conditions [], for components used in the geothermal industry [,], or to obtain high-performance coatings [].

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion
